analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to give Medicaid-style rebates to community health clinics on prescription drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a House floor vote: it sat in committee for over a year, got one subcommittee hearing in July 1992, and died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Community health centers, migrant health clinics, family planning clinics, and other federally funded clinics would get the same rebates from drug manufacturers that Medicaid already gets. Manufacturers would pay back a share of each drug's price, with the money going back to the clinics. Grants to the clinics could not be cut because of the rebates, and clinics could not resell the discounted drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients at community health centers, migrant health centers, family planning clinics, STD and drug treatment clinics, and black lung clinics — largely low-income and uninsured people — would get prescription drugs, including birth control, at lower cost, letting clinics treat more people with the same budget. Taxpayers also benefit because clinic grants stretch further.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income patients at federally funded clinics

how_it_helps.text: Covered entities — including community and migrant health centers, family planning projects, and drug and alcohol treatment clinics — could not buy drugs from any manufacturer without a rebate agreement equal to the Medicaid rebate amount [S3].
The definition of 'drug' includes over-the-counter drugs and birth control devices dispensed by the clinics, so contraception would also be discounted [S2][S3].
Federal grants to the clinics could not be reduced because of the rebates, so the savings would stay with the clinics rather than offsetting federal spending [S2][S3].
The bill also directed the Secretary to negotiate contracts aimed at clinic drug prices no higher than their September 1990 prices plus inflation, and required a report on savings achieved [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, who would pay rebates on drugs sold to the covered clinics at rates matching the Medicaid rebate formula. Clinics would bear modest new paperwork for quarterly rebate claims, and the Health and Human Services Department would administer the claims process.

drawbacks.text: The rebate-claim machinery adds administrative work: clinics must file quarterly claims with average prices paid, and the Secretary must consolidate and forward claims to manufacturers within fixed deadlines — real overhead for small clinics [S3].

Manufacturers argued then, as now, that mandatory rebate formulas can reduce revenue that funds new drug development, and a rebate tied to the Medicaid formula would extend government price-setting deeper into the market. The bill contained no direct response beyond the requirement itself [S3].
The bill prohibited covered entities from reselling rebate drugs, with a $25,000 civil penalty per violation, acknowledging the risk that discounted drugs could leak into the resale market [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: drug manufacturers would give up part of their revenue on a narrow set of federally funded clinic purchases, and clinics serving low-income patients would buy the same drugs cheaper. The main cost is administrative complexity, and the resale ban plus penalty addresses the main leakage risk. It is a modest, targeted discount mechanism rather than broad price control.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and sent to its health subcommittee, which held a hearing in July 1992, but the bill never got a markup or a floor vote and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Wyden introduced the bill on September 24, 1991, joined by Rep. Jim Cooper and four other cosponsors [S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on October 4, 1991 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment [S5].

The subcommittee held a hearing on July 31, 1992 — the only further action recorded — and the bill never advanced to a committee vote or the House floor before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers avoided paying Medicaid-style rebates on clinic drug sales, and clinics serving low-income patients kept paying higher prices.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers; clinics kept paying full price

against.what_they_did: Opposed extending mandatory Medicaid-style rebates to other purchasers; opposition to such rebate mandates was publicly and credibly reported at the time, though the congressional record for this bill does not show it.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan but small — six cosponsors split 5 Democrats and 1 Republican — and the record shows no votes, so no partisan breakdown of any decision exists.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers to pay rebates equal to the Medicaid rebate on every drug sold to covered clinics, including over-the-counter drugs and birth control devices. Clinic patients pay the resulting higher prices or get less care when clinic budgets run short.

industries.industry: Community health centers and family planning clinics
industries.note: These clinics would receive rebate payments on their drug purchases, and the bill barred any reduction in their federal grants because of the rebates, so the savings would fund more patient care.
